## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Suvaṇṇahaṁsajātaka* (Ja 136) is a story in the Jātaka collection of the Pali Canon, known in English as *The Golden Goose*. Set at Jetavana, the introductory narrative frames the tale around the greed of the nun Thullanandā ("Fat Nanda") [Fausböll 1877]. In the past narrative, the Bodhisatta was born as a golden goose who visited his impoverished former wife and three daughters, giving them one golden feather at a time to support them [Anandajoti 2010; Fausböll 1877]. Overcome by greed, his former wife forcibly plucked all his feathers at once to seize his wealth, resulting in the loss of his golden plumage [Anandajoti 2010]. The verse opens with the theme of contentment (*Yaṁ laddhaṁ tena tuṭṭhabbaṁ*) [Fausböll 1877]. At the end of the narrative, the Buddha identifies the former wife as Thullanandā, her daughters as Thullanandā's sisters, and the golden goose as himself [Fausböll 1877].

 Ute Hüsken observes that Ja 136 presents an expanded, frequently verbatim literary adaptation of this Vinaya narrative [Hüsken 1997]. Machine text-reuse searches in DharmaNexus detected no internal Pali reuses or cross-language alignments meeting threshold criteria [DharmaNexus].
